```{r setup}
# PRESENTATION LAYER ONLY. No recoding, model selection or statistical decision
# is made in this file; every value is read from the verified RDS checkpoints.
source(here::here("Scripts", "00_setup_config.R"), encoding = "UTF-8")
source(here::here("Scripts", "helpers_report.R"), encoding = "UTF-8")

ds <- load_rds(RDS$descr)           # results_04_descriptive
bv <- load_rds(RDS$bivar)           # results_05_bivariate
mp <- load_rds(RDS$mp_all)          # results_06c_modified_poisson_cPR_aPR
tb <- load_rds(RDS$tbl_obj)         # results_07_table_objects
fd <- load_rds(RDS$fig_data)        # results_07_figure_data

N    <- ds$N
pv   <- ds$prevalence
cn   <- fd$flow$counts
dg   <- mp$diagnostics
cb   <- mp$combined
bt   <- bv$table
sc   <- ds$knowledge_composite$score
lv   <- ds$knowledge_composite$level

# ---- small text helpers (formatting only) ------------------------------------------------
catn  <- function(var, level) {
  r <- ds$categorical[ds$categorical$var == var & ds$categorical$level == level, ]
  sprintf("n = %d, %.1f%%", r$n, r$pct)
}
top_level <- function(var) {
  b <- ds$categorical[ds$categorical$var == var, ]; b[which.max(b$n), ]
}
pstr <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "P < 0.001", paste0("P = ", fmt_p(p)))
ci_txt <- function(lo, hi) paste0(fmt_num(lo, 2), EN, fmt_num(hi, 2))
is_sig_pr <- function(p, lo, hi) {
  !is.na(p) & !is.na(lo) & !is.na(hi) & (p < ALPHA) & (round(lo, 2) > 1 | round(hi, 2) < 1)
}
short_contrast_name <- function(var_id, level, label) {
  lv <- gsub(">=", "\u2265", level)
  dplyr::case_when(
    var_id == "V042" ~ "high contraceptive knowledge",
    var_id == "V005" ~ "currently married or cohabiting status",
    var_id == "V046" ~ "parity of \u22653 children",
    var_id == "V048" ~ "a supportive partner",
    var_id == "V035" ~ paste0("partner communication ", tolower(lv)),
    var_id == "V004" ~ paste0("religion (", tolower(lv), ")"),
    var_id == "V047" ~ "secondary or higher education",
    TRUE ~ paste0(tolower(label), " (", tolower(lv), ")")
  )
}
pr_sentence <- function(r, type = c("aPR", "cPR"), include_stats = TRUE) {
  type <- match.arg(type)
  est <- if (type == "aPR") r$apr else r$cpr
  lo  <- if (type == "aPR") r$apr_lo else r$cpr_lo
  hi  <- if (type == "aPR") r$apr_hi else r$cpr_hi
  p   <- if (type == "aPR") r$apr_p else r$cpr_p
  nm  <- short_contrast_name(r$var_id, r$level, r$label)
  if (!include_stats) return(nm)
  sprintf("%s (%s = %s, 95%% CI %s, %s)", nm, type, fmt_num(est, 2), ci_txt(lo, hi), pstr(p))
}
sig_rows <- function(panel, type = c("aPR", "cPR"), dir = c("all", "high", "low")) {
  type <- match.arg(type); dir <- match.arg(dir)
  est <- if (type == "aPR") cb$apr else cb$cpr
  lo  <- if (type == "aPR") cb$apr_lo else cb$cpr_lo
  hi  <- if (type == "aPR") cb$apr_hi else cb$cpr_hi
  p   <- if (type == "aPR") cb$apr_p else cb$cpr_p
  keep <- cb$panel == panel & !cb$is_ref & is_sig_pr(p, lo, hi)
  if (dir == "high") keep <- keep & (est > 1)
  if (dir == "low")  keep <- keep & (est < 1)
  cb[keep, , drop = FALSE]
}
sig_list <- function(panel, type = c("aPR", "cPR"), dir = c("all", "high", "low"), include_stats = TRUE) {
  type <- match.arg(type); dir <- match.arg(dir)
  r <- sig_rows(panel, type, dir)
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return("")
  comma_and(vapply(seq_len(nrow(r)), function(i) pr_sentence(r[i, ], type, include_stats), character(1)))
}
comma_and <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) <= 1) return(paste(x, collapse = ""))
  if (length(x) == 2) return(paste(x, collapse = " and "))
  paste0(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), " and ", x[length(x)])
}

cap <- list(
  t41 = "Table 4.1. Sociodemographic and other characteristics of study participants",
  t42 = "Table 4.2. Distribution and prevalence of current modern contraceptive use",
  t43 = "Table 4.3. Knowledge of modern contraceptive methods, advantages and side effects",
  t44 = "Table 4.4. Bivariate associations between selected factors and current modern contraceptive use",
  t45 = "Table 4.5. Crude and adjusted prevalence ratios for factors associated with current modern contraceptive use",
  f41 = "Figure 4.1. Participant flow through the study, from imported records to the final analytical sample",
  f42 = paste0("Figure 4.2. Adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) and 95% confidence intervals for factors associated with current modern contraceptive use, by analysis population. Panel A presents the full sample (n = ",
               dg$n_model[dg$panel == "A"], "), and Panel B presents currently married or cohabiting women (n = ",
               dg$n_model[dg$panel == "B"], "). The vertical reference line at PR = 1 indicates the null value. Estimates are displayed on a logarithmic scale."))
```

## 4.1 Introduction

This chapter presents the findings of the study on knowledge and socio-cultural factors affecting modern contraceptive use among women of reproductive age (15–49 years) in Mkuranga District, Pwani Region. The results are organised according to the specific objectives of the study. Participant flow and the analytical sample are described first (Section 4.2), followed by the sociodemographic and other characteristics of the participants (Section 4.3). The prevalence of current modern contraceptive use is then presented (Section 4.4), followed by women's knowledge of modern contraceptive methods, their advantages and side effects (Section 4.5). Bivariate associations between selected factors and current modern contraceptive use are presented in Section 4.6, and modified Poisson regression estimating crude and adjusted prevalence ratios is presented in Section 4.7. The chapter closes with a summary of the principal findings by objective (Section 4.8).

## 4.2 Participant Flow and Analytical Sample

Figure 4.1 illustrates the flow of participants from data import to the final analytical sample. A total of `r cn$imported` records were imported from the KoboToolbox survey export. After removing `r cn$duplicates_removed` exact duplicate submissions, `r cn$eligible` unique respondents remained, all of whom met the age eligibility criterion of 15–49 years. The final analytical sample therefore comprised `r cn$final` women (`r fmt_pct(100 * cn$final / cn$planned_sample)` of the target sample of `r cn$planned_sample`). Of these, `r cn$panelB` women were currently married or cohabiting and formed the analytical subsample for partner-related analyses (Panel B).

## 4.3 Sociodemographic and Other Characteristics of Participants

Table 4.1 describes the `r N` women in the analytical sample. Their mean age was `r fmt_num(ds$continuous$mean[1], 1)` years (SD `r fmt_num(ds$continuous$sd[1], 1)`) and the largest age group was `r top_level("age_group")$level` (`r sprintf("%d, %.1f%%", top_level("age_group")$n, top_level("age_group")$pct)`). Most women had primary (`r catn("education", "Primary")`) or secondary (`r catn("education", "Secondary")`) education, and Muslims accounted for `r catn("religion", "Muslim")`. Women currently married or cohabiting accounted for `r catn("marital_status", "Currently married / Cohabiting")`, and the most common occupational status was self-employment (`r catn("occupation_status", "Self-employed")`). The median number of living children was `r fmt_num(ds$continuous$median[2], 0)` (Q1–Q3: `r fmt_num(ds$continuous$q1[2], 0)`–`r fmt_num(ds$continuous$q3[2], 0)`).

## 4.4 Prevalence of Current Modern Contraceptive Use

Table 4.2 presents the primary outcome. Of the `r pv$n_with_outcome` women with available outcome data, `r pv$n_using` were currently using a modern contraceptive method, giving a prevalence of `r fmt_pct(pv$pct_using)` (95% CI `r fmt_num(pv$ci_lo, 1)`–`r fmt_num(pv$ci_hi, 1)`). Among currently married or cohabiting women the prevalence was `r fmt_pct(pv$in_union$pct)` (95% CI `r fmt_num(pv$in_union$ci[1], 1)`–`r fmt_num(pv$in_union$ci[2], 1)`).

## 4.5 Knowledge of Modern Contraceptive Methods, Advantages and Side Effects

Table 4.3 presents item-level responses across the 18 knowledge items alongside the composite knowledge score and knowledge level classification. Among the six modern contraceptive methods, awareness was highest for `r tolower(ds$knowledge_items$item[which.max(ds$knowledge_items$pct_yes[1:6])])` (`r fmt_pct(max(ds$knowledge_items$pct_yes[1:6]))`) and lowest for `r tolower(ds$knowledge_items$item[which.min(ds$knowledge_items$pct_yes[1:6])])` (`r fmt_pct(min(ds$knowledge_items$pct_yes[1:6]))`). The most widely known advantage was "`r tolower(ds$knowledge_items$item[6 + which.max(ds$knowledge_items$pct_yes[7:14])])`" (`r fmt_pct(max(ds$knowledge_items$pct_yes[7:14]))`), whereas the least known was "`r tolower(ds$knowledge_items$item[6 + which.min(ds$knowledge_items$pct_yes[7:14])])`" (`r fmt_pct(min(ds$knowledge_items$pct_yes[7:14]))`). Of the four listed side effects, "`r tolower(ds$knowledge_items$item[14 + which.max(ds$knowledge_items$pct_yes[15:18])])`" was the most frequently recognised (`r fmt_pct(max(ds$knowledge_items$pct_yes[15:18]))`). Across all 18 items, the composite knowledge score (range `r fmt_num(sc$min, 0)`–`r fmt_num(sc$max, 0)`) had a mean of `r fmt_num(sc$mean, 2)` (SD `r fmt_num(sc$sd, 2)`) and a median of `r fmt_num(sc$median, 0)` (Q1–Q3: `r fmt_num(sc$q1, 0)`–`r fmt_num(sc$q3, 0)`). Using the sample mean (`r fmt_num(sc$mean, 2)`) as the cut-off, `r lv$n[2]` women (`r fmt_pct(lv$pct[2])`) had high knowledge (≥ mean) and `r lv$n[1]` (`r fmt_pct(lv$pct[1])`) had low knowledge (< mean).

## 4.6 Bivariate Associations with Current Modern Contraceptive Use

Table 4.4 presents the bivariate associations in three sections: sociodemographic and knowledge factors in the full sample (Section A), partner-related factors among women currently married or cohabiting (Section B), and socio-cultural factors in the full sample (Section C). `r sig_n <- length(unique(bt$var_id[bt$p_value < ALPHA])); if (sig_n == 0) "None of the tested factors was significantly associated with current use at the 5% level." else paste0("Of the ", length(unique(bt$var_id)), " tested factors, ", sig_n, " were significantly associated with current use at the 5% level:")` `r s <- bt %>% filter(p_value < ALPHA) %>% distinct(var_id, .keep_all = TRUE); paste(sprintf("%s (%s, %s = %s, %s)", tolower(s$label), s$statistic, s$effect_name, fmt_num(s$effect_size, 2), pstr(s$p_value)), collapse = "; ")`. `r pn <- bt %>% filter(p_value >= ALPHA) %>% distinct(var_id, label); if (nrow(pn) > 0) paste0("No significant association was observed for ", comma_and(tolower(pn$label)), ".") else ""` In the partner-related section, women who reported that their partner supported contraceptive use had a higher proportion of current use (`r fmt_pct(bt$pct_present[bt$var_id == "V048" & bt$level == "Supportive"])`) than women whose partner did not support or whose partner's view was unknown (`r fmt_pct(bt$pct_present[bt$var_id == "V048" & bt$level == "Not supportive / Don't Know"])`).

## 4.7 Factors Associated with Current Modern Contraceptive Use: Modified Poisson Regression

Table 4.5 presents crude prevalence ratios (cPRs) and adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) for factors associated with current modern contraceptive use. Panel A presents findings for the full sample of `r dg$n_model[dg$panel == "A"]` women, including `r dg$events[dg$panel == "A"]` current users, while Panel B presents findings restricted to the `r dg$n_model[dg$panel == "B"]` currently married or cohabiting women, including `r dg$events[dg$panel == "B"]` current users.

```{r t45cap, results='asis'}

```

```{r t45}
make_ft(tb$t45, font_size = 8)
```

```{r t45notes, results='asis'}
print_notes(tb$t45)
```

After multivariable adjustment, the prevalence of current modern contraceptive use in the full sample (Panel A) was significantly higher for `r sig_list("A", "aPR", "high")`. Among currently married or cohabiting women (Panel B), adjusted prevalence was significantly higher for `r sig_list("B", "aPR", "high")` and lower for `r sig_list("B", "aPR", "low")` (Figure 4.2).

## 4.8 Summary of Principal Findings

**Objective 1: To determine the prevalence of modern contraceptive use.** The prevalence of current modern contraceptive use was `r fmt_pct(pv$pct_using)` (95% CI `r fmt_num(pv$ci_lo, 1)`–`r fmt_num(pv$ci_hi, 1)`; n = `r pv$n_using` of `r pv$n_with_outcome`), and `r fmt_pct(pv$in_union$pct)` (95% CI `r fmt_num(pv$in_union$ci[1], 1)`–`r fmt_num(pv$in_union$ci[2], 1)`) among currently married or cohabiting women.

**Objective 2: To assess the level of knowledge of modern contraceptive methods.** Awareness of individual methods ranged from `r fmt_pct(min(ds$knowledge_items$pct_yes[1:6]), 0)` to `r fmt_pct(max(ds$knowledge_items$pct_yes[1:6]), 0)`, whereas knowledge of individual advantages and side effects ranged from `r fmt_pct(min(ds$knowledge_items$pct_yes[7:18]), 0)` to `r fmt_pct(max(ds$knowledge_items$pct_yes[7:18]), 0)`. The mean composite knowledge score across the 18 items was `r fmt_num(sc$mean, 2)` (SD `r fmt_num(sc$sd, 2)`), with `r lv$n[2]` (`r fmt_pct(lv$pct[2])`) classified as having high knowledge (≥ mean) and `r lv$n[1]` (`r fmt_pct(lv$pct[1])`) as having low knowledge (< mean).

**Objective 3: To determine the association between socio-cultural factors and modern contraceptive use.** In bivariate analysis, `r comma_and(tolower(unique(s$label)))` `r if (length(unique(s$label)) == 1) "was" else "were"` significantly associated with current modern contraceptive use. In multivariable modified Poisson regression, `r sig_list("A", "aPR", "high", FALSE)` remained significantly associated with higher use in the full sample (Panel A), while among currently married or cohabiting women (Panel B), `r sig_list("B", "aPR", "high", FALSE)` were associated with higher use and `r sig_list("B", "aPR", "low", FALSE)` with lower use.
